cases.brief: Kestrel Staffing places warehouse and logistics workers across three regions and wants software that ranks incoming applications so recruiters see the strongest candidates first. The managing director came back from a trade show convinced the agency is falling behind, and has promised the board a pilot within ninety days. You have been hired as AI governance lead before anything is built. A contractor has already pitched a deep-learning ranking engine in a slide deck, and an analyst has started copying ten years of old placement records into a spreadsheet to use as training data. This week your task is to put planning back in sequence: purpose, context, governance approach and the people affected first, technical build decisions later, and no money committed to the contractor's design until then.

steps.q: Nobody at Kestrel has yet agreed what problem the ranking tool is supposed to solve. As planning begins, which activity should come first?
options: Set out the problem to be solved and weigh costs against benefits, including whether AI is needed
Put the contractor's candidate models through testing, evaluation, verification and validation
Commission an algorithmic impact assessment that builds on the agency's existing privacy reviews
Work out how rejected candidates will be able to challenge or appeal a ranking decision
steps.answer: Set out the problem to be solved and weigh costs against benefits, including whether AI is needed
steps.why: Planning starts by justifying the project: what outcome Kestrel wants, what it will cost, what it will gain, and whether a non-AI approach would do the job just as well. Testing and validation, impact assessment and appeal routes are all legitimate governance work, but each presupposes a defined system and a decision to go ahead. Doing them before the project has a justified purpose puts the lifecycle in the wrong order.

steps.q: The managing director's case for the tool counts only recruiter hours saved and faster fill rates. What does a properly scoped cost-benefit analysis add?
options: Longer-range forecasts of the recruiter hours saved over five years
Effects on people and society, such as which applicants get ranked lower
A fuller breakdown of cloud hosting, licensing and support costs
Benchmarks of the fill rates achieved by rival staffing agencies
steps.answer: Effects on people and society, such as which applicants get ranked lower
steps.why: An analysis that stops at internal efficiency ignores the people the system acts on. For a candidate-ranking tool the central question is who gets pushed down the list, and whether that is fair and lawful; it belongs in the analysis next to the savings. The other three options only stretch the same inward-looking financial view the managing director started with.

steps.q: The contractor wants the deep-learning design approved this week so work can begin. At which point in the lifecycle should the model architecture be settled?
options: During planning, since choosing the architecture is a core planning output
During design and development, once planning has been completed
By the governance committee, which should pick the architecture itself
By the hosting provider, which knows what its platform runs best
steps.answer: During design and development, once planning has been completed
steps.why: Planning fixes the objective, assumptions, operating context and governance approach; it does not choose a model architecture. Whether the ranking engine ends up as a neural network, a gradient-boosted model or a simple scoring rule is decided in design and development, after planning has said what the system must achieve. The governance committee sets guardrails rather than picking techniques, and a hosting provider has no say in the choice.

steps.q: Planning closes and design begins. Kestrel's stakeholder map lists the analytics team, the governance committee, the hosting provider and job applicants. When the tool's risks are assessed, whose perspective should carry the most weight?
options: The analytics team, who know best what the ranking model can and cannot do
The job applicants, whose chances of being placed depend on the ranking
Compliance staff, who judge the legal and regulatory exposure of the tool
Senior leadership, who own the agency's overall appetite for risk
steps.answer: The job applicants, whose chances of being placed depend on the ranking
steps.why: Stakeholder mapping is meant to steer risk assessment toward the people who live with the system's outputs. At Kestrel those are the applicants: an unfairly low ranking can cost someone a job, and none of the internal groups bears that consequence. Technical, compliance and leadership views all belong in the process, but they are inputs, not the people most exposed.

steps.q: In design, Kestrel has to choose between logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees and a neural network for the ranking model. Who should own that decision?
options: Kestrel's own analytics team, who understand the data and the performance targets
The governance committee, because picking an algorithm is itself a risk decision
The hosting provider, since it knows which models run efficiently on its platform
The outside contractor who first pitched the deep-learning ranking engine
steps.answer: Kestrel's own analytics team, who understand the data and the performance targets
steps.why: Choosing an algorithm type is a technical judgement for the people who understand the data, the business context and the performance requirements, which here means Kestrel's own analytics team. The governance committee defines the risk limits the chosen approach must respect but does not select techniques. Note the difference from step 3: that step was about when architecture is decided, while this one is about who decides. A hosting provider or contractor can advise, but the authority stays inside Kestrel.

cases.brief: Lowmoor Borough Council is building a model that reads incoming adult social-care referrals and suggests an urgency level; any referral the model is unsure about goes straight to a senior social worker. The council has already adopted AI principles, set up an oversight board, formed a multidisciplinary project team, and written policies covering standards, workflows and acceptable risk levels. A systems integrator will build the model, a hosting company will run it, and it will learn from the council's own case records plus anonymised referral data shared by a neighbouring authority. As the council's AIGP, you are scoping the impact assessment that must be finished before training and testing start, and you need to be precise about what that assessment is for and what it is not.

steps.q: A project officer's status note says the impact assessment is there "to show the board what the council will gain from the model." How should you correct the note?
options: Its job is to identify and quantify the gains the council expects from the model
Its job is to foresee the harms the model could cause and put controls around them
Its job is to record which teams and suppliers are accountable for each part of the model
Its job is to assess whether building the model could expose the council to legal claims
steps.answer: Its job is to foresee the harms the model could cause and put controls around them
steps.why: Used as a management tool, the impact assessment is about what could go wrong: residents wrongly marked as low urgency, unequal treatment of particular groups, misuse of sensitive records. It is not a tally of benefits. IAPP's own guidance describes its purpose more widely, as helping an organisation understand the good and the bad a system may bring (FSG p.6/8, Q2), so the two framings are compatible at different levels; this step concerns what the assessment is built to control. An accountability register and a legal-exposure review are useful documents, but they are different instruments.

steps.q: Lowmoor's information governance team already runs a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) on every data project. Rather than start the AI impact assessment from nothing, what should the team do?
options: Adapt the existing data protection impact assessment into the AI impact assessment
Adapt an existing health and safety risk assessment, since resident safety is the main worry
Adapt an existing cyber-security assessment, since the model handles sensitive case records
Adapt an existing environmental assessment, since hosting the model consumes electricity
steps.answer: Adapt the existing data protection impact assessment into the AI impact assessment
steps.why: A DPIA is the closest ready-made template because both instruments examine risk arising from how data is used. Extending that method into the ethical, social and legal questions specific to AI is far easier than starting from scratch. Safety and security assessments each look through a single narrow lens, and an environmental assessment answers a question this document is not responsible for.

steps.q: The triage model does one narrow job and is not a general-purpose system. Which item is NOT required content in its impact assessment?
options: How the model could affect the privacy of residents and their families
Where the training data came from, including the neighbouring authority's records
Whether the model's urgency scores differ unfairly between groups of residents
How much electricity the model draws each time it scores a referral
steps.answer: How much electricity the model draws each time it scores a referral
steps.why: Impact assessments focus on risks to people, to the organisation and to legal compliance: privacy, lawful data sourcing and unfair outcomes. For a narrow system like this one, electricity use falls outside that required core, although it is a fair topic in wider sustainability discussions. The other three items are standard content whatever the system's scope.

steps.q: Before the integrator trains and tests the model, which single step does most to reduce the chance that it treats some groups of residents unfairly?
options: Obtain a larger batch of referral data from the neighbouring authority
Hire an independent auditor to review the model once it is finished
Complete the impact assessment before any training starts
Offer rewards to anyone who reports bias after a limited rollout
steps.answer: Complete the impact assessment before any training starts
steps.why: Doing the impact assessment before training exposes discrimination risk while data sourcing, labelling and design can still change, which is the whole reason for doing it early. Extra data does not cure a badly framed problem, and an independent audit or a bias bounty can only detect problems in a model that already exists.

cases.brief: Fernhill Energy, a household gas and electricity supplier, plans to launch "Juno" next month: an in-house large language model that explains bills, sets up payment plans and passes complicated calls to human agents. The legal team fears liability for wrong advice about debt; the communications team fears headlines if Juno mistreats vulnerable customers. Before go-live you must decide whether Juno is genuinely ready, using the evidence from its shadow run, choosing the right document for each audience, and separating what customers are told from what stays inside Fernhill.
cases.citation: SG (shadow mode); SG (model card vs system dossier); SG (retrain = new release)

steps.q: For four weeks Juno has run in shadow mode, drafting answers to real customer messages in the background while agents sent the actual replies. The results were recorded. What does this mainly show?
options: That Juno is ready to deploy, because it faced live conditions without affecting customers
That Juno's architecture performs well, whether or not any results were written down
That future testing can be handed to an outside firm without any internal review
That Fernhill now has enough evidence to announce the launch to the press
steps.answer: That Juno is ready to deploy, because it faced live conditions without affecting customers
steps.why: Shadow running with recorded outcomes counts as release-readiness evidence because the model meets real traffic and real edge cases without any customer bearing the cost of a mistake, much like running a new system in parallel before cutover. Claims of strong performance mean nothing to an auditor without recorded results; handing testing to an outsider with no internal review gives away governance's own responsibility; and a press announcement is marketing, not evidence (SG).

steps.q: Before signing off, Fernhill's lawyers open Juno's model card. Which section matters most from a governance standpoint?
options: The uses Juno was designed for and the limits its developers identified
Juno's accuracy, precision and recall figures from evaluation runs
The origin, volume and make-up of the data Juno was trained on
Estimates of the power Juno consumes and the emissions involved
steps.answer: The uses Juno was designed for and the limits its developers identified
steps.why: Intended use and known limitations mark out where Juno can responsibly be used. Deploying a model beyond that boundary is a frequent source of governance failure and legal exposure, which is precisely the lawyers' concern. Evaluation figures and training-data details belong in the same card but offer little protection if the model is used outside its tested scope, and energy use is a sustainability matter rather than the main readiness risk here.

steps.q: A developer asks why Juno needs both a model card and a separate system dossier, since the two seem to overlap. Where does the line between them actually fall?
options: The model card profiles one model version; the system dossier covers the full production setting, such as architecture, data lineage, monitoring and conformity evidence
They contain the same information, so Fernhill should retire one of them and save the effort of keeping two documents up to date
The system dossier is the summary published for customers, whereas the model card is an internal document that never leaves the engineering team
The model card is limited to describing training data, while the system dossier is limited to reporting performance metrics for each release
steps.answer: The model card profiles one model version; the system dossier covers the full production setting, such as architecture, data lineage, monitoring and conformity evidence
steps.why: The two documents are scoped differently by design. The model card is tied to a specific version and explains what that model is and how it should be used. The system dossier explains how the model sits within the live system, including the monitoring and conformity evidence the card does not repeat. Calling them duplicates, dividing them by public versus internal audience, or dividing them by data versus metrics all get the boundary wrong (SG).

steps.q: The communications team is drafting Juno's customer-facing disclosure. Which item should be left out?
options: What Juno is for and which kinds of request it handles
Fernhill's in-house prompt and fine-tuning techniques
A statement that Juno meets the applicable legal rules
The known weaknesses and limits of Juno's answers
steps.answer: Fernhill's in-house prompt and fine-tuning techniques
steps.why: Customers are owed an explanation of purpose, legal compliance and honest limitations, not Fernhill's trade secrets. Disclosure duties weigh public understanding against the organisation's legitimate interest in protecting its intellectual property, so purpose, compliance and limitations go in while the underlying techniques stay internal.

steps.q: Juno goes live. Four months later, monitoring shows its behaviour has shifted enough that the team retrains it on newer data. Before the retrained version returns to production, what level of review does it need?
options: The same review as a first release: fairness, robustness and accuracy re-tested, documentation updated, and formal governance approval before deployment
A lighter, internal-only sign-off, on the basis that retraining is routine maintenance rather than a genuine new launch
No further review at all, provided the retrained version's accuracy matches or beats that of the version it replaces
Only a brief engineering smoke test, because the model card written for the original release still describes it correctly
steps.answer: The same review as a first release: fairness, robustness and accuracy re-tested, documentation updated, and formal governance approval before deployment
steps.why: Retraining changes how the model reaches its outputs, so governance treats the result as a new release rather than a patch: full re-validation, refreshed documentation and transparency material, and formal approval before it serves customers again. This is separate from Case D's rule that containment comes first. Case D is about not retraining, or doing anything else, before a live incident is contained; this step says that whenever retraining happens, whether prompted by an incident or scheduled, the new version needs first-release rigour on its way back into service (SG).

cases.brief: It is 6:15pm on the Thursday before a bank holiday. Corrie Mutual's automated claims-approval model has been live for nine months and settles roughly 2,500 home and motor claims each day. A governance alert fires: recall has fallen steeply, and a drift test shows that incoming claim data no longer resembles the data the model was trained on. In the same alert feed, a slower signal has been building for weeks: a fairness check shows claimants from one ethnic group are approved 1.4% less often than others, below Corrie's 1.5% escalation threshold but rising. You are the governance lead on call, and every decision you make over the next hour and the next month will be on the record.

steps.q: The alert for falling recall and shifted inputs has just triggered. What should happen first?
options: Take the model out of the live claims flow, route claims to human handlers, and inform legal and compliance
Investigate whether the shift is real or a data-pipeline fault before taking any action on the model
Trigger the automatic retraining job straight away, using the latest production claims data
Post a notice to customers about a service problem and promise a swift investigation
steps.answer: Take the model out of the live claims flow, route claims to human handlers, and inform legal and compliance
steps.why: While a degraded model is still deciding real claims, the first priority is to stop further damage: remove it from the live flow and fall back to human handling before anything else. Diagnosis matters, but not while the model keeps making decisions; retraining automatically on the same shifted data may entrench the fault; and a customer notice issued before containment and investigation gets the order wrong.

steps.q: A colleague argues that the team should diagnose the cause first, because you cannot fix what you do not yet understand. Why is that the wrong sequence here?
options: Because containment, isolating the system so it stops making faulty decisions, must precede investigation; halting harm that is still happening comes first
Because diagnosis should only begin after the model has been fully retrained on clean data and redeployed
Because informing affected customers must always happen before any technical step is taken
Because rolling back to an earlier model version is the only acceptable opening move in any incident
steps.answer: Because containment, isolating the system so it stops making faulty decisions, must precede investigation; halting harm that is still happening comes first
steps.why: Incident response puts containment first because Corrie's model is still harming claimants with every decision it makes: stop the damage, then diagnose it. Investigation is necessary but comes second. Leading with customer messaging, or assuming a rollback is always the answer without first halting the live harm, skips the step that actually protects people right now.

steps.q: While that incident is being contained, an analyst raises the slower bias signal: a 1.4% approval gap for claimants from one ethnic group, below the 1.5% escalation threshold. What is the best response?
options: Open formal incident response now, even though the gap sits below the threshold, because a protected group is affected
Log it as a near miss, test more often, and escalate only if the gap keeps growing or crosses the line
Put it on the agenda for the next quarterly governance meeting and consult stakeholders before escalating
Quietly apply interim compensating controls and hold escalation in reserve until the bias is confirmed
steps.answer: Open formal incident response now, even though the gap sits below the threshold, because a protected group is affected
steps.why: An escalation threshold sets a trigger for routine monitoring; it does not cap judgement. Where a protected group is affected, governance should escalate even when the figure sits under the line, because that is the defensible position if a regulator later asks why a known disparity was left alone. Waiting for the number to reach 1.5%, waiting for a scheduled meeting, or handling it quietly all treat the threshold as permission to delay, which is the exposure the rule exists to remove.

steps.q: Both incidents have now been contained and investigated. In what order should they be closed?
options: Record both in the central AI incident register first, then hold a blameless review and run corrective and preventive action on the findings
Skip the formal record and go straight to a full retraining of the model, since retraining is the real remedy for both problems
Close both tickets once the monitoring dashboards show normal readings again, without holding any formal review
Hold off telling cross-functional stakeholders until every corrective action is complete, so as not to cause alarm
steps.answer: Record both in the central AI incident register first, then hold a blameless review and run corrective and preventive action on the findings
steps.why: Formal logging is the immediate step that sets everything else in motion: investigation, stakeholder notification, and corrective and preventive action (CAPA). A blameless review that still assigns owners for fixes is how findings become lasting process change rather than a one-off repair. Going straight to retraining, or closing tickets because the dashboards look normal, leaves no auditable record, and delaying stakeholder notice until CAPA is finished reverses an order governance relies on (SG).
